articleBlocks: I first read the set as 'travel essentials'—keycards, toiletries, coffee makers all sound like things you'd want on a trip.
But then I hit 'continental breakfast' and 'room service'.
Those aren't things you pack; they're services you receive.
That contradiction made me rethink the whole list.
If the clues are a mix of objects and services, they probably point to a location.
Keycards unlock doors at a hotel.
Electric kettles or coffee makers sit on the hotel room desk.
Toiletries appear in the bathroom, often in tiny bottles.
Continental breakfast shows up in the lobby or dining area each morning.
Room service brings meals right to your door.
The answer clicked: things associated with hotels.
It wasn't a packing list at all—it was a list of what a hotel provides.
The set is clean because every clue is a standard part of the hotel experience.
Once I stopped thinking about what I carry and started thinking about what a place offers, the solve felt obvious.
solutionNarrative: I tested Keycards first, and the useful detail is the lifecycle: the front desk issues one card for one room at arrival, and the same card stops working at checkout. That borrow-and-return cycle is what separates a lodging keycard from an office pass, so the opening clue already pointed past a packing list.

I checked Electric kettles / coffee makers next. Both machines sit in hotel rooms by default, restocked with pods, cups, and sugar sachets between bookings; a home kitchen buys whichever model the owner prefers. The hotel signal is standardization across every room, not the appliance itself.

Toiletries fit the hotel reading through housekeeping: small bottles and wrapped soaps are placed by someone else, used briefly, and replaced after each checkout. That resupply loop is a hospitality convention, not a product a guest packed.

Continental breakfast was the deciding line. The term names a lodging meal plan of pastries, fruit, coffee, and juice included with the room rate; a boarding gate does not serve one, and an apartment does not include one by default. Once I placed that clue, the hotel frame stopped being a guess.

Room service closed the loop: a guest orders from a hotel menu by phone, and the charge lands on the room bill. With all five entries accounted for, the board reads as one category of objects and services a property provides during a stay rather than five unrelated words.
